subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Wireless EV Charging
description: Learn Wireless EV Charging in one minute.

hook.text: Imagine pulling into a parking spot and your car starts charging—no plug, no cable, no effort.

buildup.text: Wireless charging uses magnetic resonance to transfer energy through an air gap to a pad under the car.

discovery.text: Efficiency is around 90–93%—close to wired charging, though a bit slower.

twist.text: Some cities are testing charging coils embedded in roads—EVs could charge while driving.

climax.text: BMW and Genesis already offer wireless charging pads for select models in some markets.

punchline.text: The future of charging might be not thinking about it.

quiz.question: How does wireless EV charging transfer energy?

details.summary: Wireless EV charging uses electromagnetic induction to transfer power through the air from a pad on the ground to a receiver on the car's underside, eliminating cables and enabling charging while parked or even driving.
details.whyItMatters: Wireless charging could make EVs as convenient as parking. If roads themselves could charge vehicles while driving, range anxiety and battery size requirements would both diminish dramatically.
takeaways: Inductive charging transfers power wirelessly through a short air gap
Efficiency reaches 90 to 93 percent, close to wired charging
Dynamic wireless charging on roads is being tested in several countries

faq.question: How efficient is wireless EV charging compared to plugging in?
faq.answer: Current wireless systems achieve 90 to 93 percent efficiency, compared to 95 percent for wired charging. The small efficiency loss is offset by the convenience of automatic, effortless charging whenever the car is parked.

faq.question: Could roads charge EVs while they drive?
faq.answer: Pilot projects in Sweden, Italy, and Michigan are testing dynamic charging embedded in road surfaces. The technology works but is extremely expensive to install at scale. Widespread deployment is likely decades away.
